t: The Lakota, whose name means “allies”, are the westernmost of the Seven Council Fires of the Sioux; pushed west onto the Plains, they became horse-mounted bison hunters and made the Black Hills their home by the 1770s.

The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty closed the Black Hills to white settlement, but after gold was found there in 1874 war followed, and despite the Lakota and Cheyenne victory at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, resistance was broken by 1877.

In 1890 Sitting Bull was killed and the 7th Cavalry massacred Lakota at Wounded Knee; the tribes still refuse the 1980 Supreme Court award for the Black Hills, because accepting it would end their claim to the land.
dyk: When the Lewis and Clark Expedition met the Sicangu in 1804, warriors seized a boat’s cable and both sides readied their weapons, until the Sicangu leader Black Buffalo let go and invited the Americans upriver under Sicangu escort.
ev: The Lewis and Clark Expedition meets the Sicangu near the mouth of the Bad River, and a standoff ends when Black Buffalo grants the Americans passage
The Fort Laramie Treaty recognises Lakota title to nearly 100,000 square miles north of the North Platte in return for roads and military posts
General William S. Harney’s troops attack a Lakota and Cheyenne village at Blue Water Creek, killing at least 86 and taking 70 women and children captive
Red Cloud leads the Lakota and their allies to victory in Red Cloud’s War, and the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty establishes the Great Sioux Reservation
Custer’s expedition confirms gold in the Black Hills, and prospectors flood in against the terms of the 1868 treaty
Lakota and Cheyenne forces under Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull defeat Custer at the Battle of the Little Bighorn
Sitting Bull is killed at Standing Rock, and two weeks later the 7th Cavalry kills at least 270 Lakota in the Wounded Knee Massacre
In United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians the Supreme Court awards $122 million for the Black Hills, which the tribes refuse

f.homeland: The northern Great Plains, with the Black Hills as the spiritual centre of their territory; earlier the upper Mississippi region and the western Great Lakes; today chiefly the Pine Ridge, Rosebud, Lower Brule, Cheyenne River and Standing Rock reservations in South Dakota, with communities in North Dakota, Nebraska, Montana, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
f.period: In the upper Mississippi region in the late 16th and early 17th centuries; pushed onto the Plains in the mid- to late 17th century; horses from the early 18th century; across the Missouri from about 1750 and in the Black Hills by the 1770s; the treaties and wars with the United States, 1825–1890; the reservation era to the present.
f.known: the seven bands of the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, the Seven Council Fires; winter counts; the sacred buffalo calf pipe of White Buffalo Calf Woman; horse-mounted bison hunting and the camp circle; the Battle of the Little Bighorn; Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse and Red Cloud; the Wounded Knee Massacre; the refusal of payment for the Black Hills
f.sources: Lakota winter counts (waníyetu wówapi) such as the Battiste Good count, and the American Horse ledger; Lakota oral tradition, as drawn on by Joseph M. Marshall III; the journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition; US treaties and army reports; photographs of the Wounded Knee burial; the fieldwork of the linguist Ella Deloria.
